seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: I do not understand your allusion to autumn. Do you intend to go to Italy ? As soon as Mr Quinn’s remittance or my next instalment of money arrives in a few days I shall send my wife and family for the holidays to Lago Maggiore : and perhaps I shall go there too afterwards. I did not receive any letter from Mr Quinn. Has he now all the acts of the play ? If not, please send him acts two and three. If they are lost I shall recopy them for him. As soon as I hear from him I shall let you know but apart from that if you have any intention of travelling (I do not urge you to do so in present circumstances) I should be very glad to know your itinerary.

I did not get Mr Eliot’s book nor the number of Poetry
with your poem in it. Perhaps they will come later. I got the June Little Review with your cheerful dialogue in it and Yeats’s verses . It is a long time since I had the pleasure of reading anything of his. I want to know whether he read Exiles
and whether the Abbey Theatre rejected it definitely. I ask because the Stage Society sent back the typescript after having kept it for nearly a year – without explanation or comment. I am sorry you do not like Exiles . I suppose Mr Quinn does not like it either. I sent the MS however at his request. As for having it typed a third time and sent on it is a useless expense. I have already paid about £12 typing expenses. Mr Richards writes he “hopes to publish it in January”. It is very difficult to get things printed, he says. I shall ask my agent to urge him to set it at once and then perhaps the typescript which he has could be sent on to New York. As usual I have to write the same thing several times to several people and in the end half of my instructions are badly executed.

I believe that your fears for the reception of Exiles are caused by your friendly interest in me. For my part I do not see how its reception, favourable or otherwise, can influence me or what I write. I wrote a month ago a long letter to Mr Quinn in reply to one of his. In it I told him the story of my books and I told him I owed their publication to you and, that being settled, he can draw his own conclusions. The sales of my novel come to about 500 copies. Such a sale after such a press is an utter fiasco: I beg you to believe that I consider you who helped me when nobody else would do so apart from the other critics. I am grateful to the score of men of letters who have written well of the book after it was published but this does not compensate for the fiasco. As regards Ulysses
I write and think and write and think all day and part of the night. It goes on as it has been going these five or six years. Buth the ingredients will not fuse until they have reached a certain temperature.

I enclose some press notices. Yours comes first as only begetter of the book. A notice appeared in the London Greek journal
Εσπερία
(29 June) written by my friend Mr Phocas , descendant of the ancient emperor and a countryman of Ulysses, who, he says, was born on Santa Mavra . You will notice that he announces to the Hellenic world my about-to-be-published epos as a wonderful version of Homer’s story. He is laughing in his sleeve, I believe. But his intentions are good and I sent a note of thanks to the editor but alas sent it to a wrong address. I suppose the person who received it is rather puzzled. I hope Mr Davray will keep his word about reviewing the book in the Mercure de France. I shall not bore you about my tiresome tiresome tiresome self and health except to say pianissimo that my neck is swollen. I have written to Mr Archer and to Mr Symons about Exiles and a Dutch journalist here who is going to review the novel in an Amsterdam paper has written to Mr Grein about it. These reviews are of course almost useless. I shall also close this letter and post it.

lg.l: Now let awhile my messmates be
In Dublin as an Irish jew.
With them I’ll sit, with them I’ll drink

l.seg: Nor heed what press and pressman think

lg.l: Nor leave their rockbound house of joy
For Helen or for windy Troy.

div.note: Pound wrote on 17 July 1917 that JJ would receive a copy of Pound’s volume of poems, Lustra, set to appear in the fall of 1917 in New York, “if it, you, and I survive till late autumn” (Pound/Joyce 122). Two impressions of Lustra were printed in New York, one for private circulation, which John Quinn began distributing in September 1917; the other a public edition issued by Alfred A. Knopf in October 1917. Pound wanted JJ to have one of the American impressions, rather than either of the English impressions issued by Elkin Mathews in 1916, because the American versions contained his “Three Cantos of a Poem of Some Length,” revised from their appearance in Poetry, vol. 10, nos. 3-5 (June, July, August 1917): 113-21, 180-88, 248-54. The American impressions of Lustra also restored poems that Mathews and his printer considered too risqué for publication in Britain, especially after the suppression of D.H. Lawrence’s The Rainbow in late 1915. For accounts of these early cantos and their relationship to Pound’s epic poem, The Cantos, see JJ to Pound, 30 March 1917, notes, and 7 July 1917, notes.

JJ was still puzzled by what Pound had meant when he wrote Nora Barnacle on 7 May 1917: “I shall go to the Lago di Garda after the war, unless I am destroyed, and I shall manage to pass through Zurich or Italy redeemed or wherever J.J. is at that time” (Pound/Joyce 115). See JJ to Pound, 5 June 1917, notes.

The New York lawyer John Quinn, a collector of modern art and literary manuscripts, had arranged to purchase items from JJ, including the manuscript of his play Exiles and the setting copy used for the American edition of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) (see JJ to Pound, 19 March 1917, notes). Pound wrote on 17 July 1917 that Quinn had sent JJ “an advance” on the Exiles manuscript (Pound/Joyce 121). When Quinn finally received acts two and three of Exiles, he sent JJ, on 18 August 1917, a “Zurich draft for 522.50 francs, being the equivalent of £25,” which did not reach JJ until mid-September (Myron Schwartzman, “‘Quinnigan’s Quake!’ John Quinn’s Letters to James Joyce, 1916-1920,” Bulletin of Research in the Humanities, vol. 81, no. 2 [Summer 1978]: 231).

JJ learned in February 1917 from London solicitors that an anonymous “admirer of [his] writing” had gifted him £200, to be paid in £50 installments in May, August, November, and the next February (LII 389). JJ thought that Pound was involved, but the admirer was later revealed to be Harriet Shaw Weaver.

Lago Maggiore is a large lake on the south side of the Alps. JJ was planning to winter with his family in Locarno, a Swiss town on the northern shore of the lake. Nora Barnacle with their two children, Lucia and Giorgio, went ahead, but she returned to Zurich after JJ suffered symptoms of glaucoma following a severe attack of lumbago there on 18 August 1917 (SL 226-27). Once he had sufficiently recovered from eye surgery, he and the family went to Locarno in October 1917 and stayed there until January 1918.

Quinn cabled Pound on 15 August 1917 that he had received acts two and three of the manuscript of JJ’s Exiles. Pound enclosed Quinn’s cablegram in his letter to JJ of 15 August 1917 (Pound/Joyce 123).

New York Times headlines from this period give an idea of the level of ferocity the war had reached on land and at sea: “French Capture Lines at Verdun” (18 July 1917, p. 1); “French Repulse German Attacks on Aisne Front,” “Chancellor Justifies U-Boat War … Vast Tonnage Sunk or Disabled” (20 July 1917, p. 1); “German Airmen Kill 11 in England; One Raider Falls,” “Mutiny on Russian Front Spreads; North Galicia Army in Retreat; Germans at Gates of Tarnopol,” “Germans Assault Craonne Heights” (23 July 1917, p. 1); “Teutons Strike from the Baltic to the Black Sea” (25 July 1917, p. 1).

T. S. Eliot’s Prufrock and Other Observations was published in June 1917 by the Egoist Press in an edition partially subsidized by Ezra and Dorothy Pound. JJ received his copy on 22 October 1917 (LIII 510).
Pound’s “Three Cantos,” an early, tentative approach to his epic poem, appeared in Poetry, vol. 10, nos. 3-5 (June, July, August 1917): 113-21, 180-88, 248-54.

The Little Review, vol. 4, no. 2 (June 1917): 14-21, printed Pound’s “An Anachronism at Chinon,” an imaginary conversation between François Rabelais (ca. 1490-1553) and a present-day American student who resembles Pound in his attitudes and expression. The two men compare their respective ages’ views of obscenity, censorship, and morality. The student complains – probably thinking of JJ’s fiction and Pound’s poetry – that “let a novelist mention a privvy [sic], or a poet the rear side of a woman, and the whole town reeks with an uproar,” and that “clear and clean realism” brings down the censors (18).

The same number contained new poems by W.B. Yeats (1865-1939): “The Wild Swans at Coole,” “Presences,” “Men Improve with the Years,” “A Deep Sworn Vow,” “The Collar-Bone of a Hare,” “Broken Dreams,” and “In Memory” (9-13). With a further contribution by Wyndham Lewis, Pound was making good his promise, as foreign editor, to bring the best, most innovative work to The Little Review.

Although Yeats, enthusiastic after reading A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, initially thought the Dublin Abbey Theatre might stage Exiles, he wrote JJ on 26 August 1917 that “it is a type of work we have never played well” since it was “too far from the folk drama.” He thought it “[not] at all so good” as A Portrait (LII 405).
For the failed efforts to interest the London-based Stage Society in producing JJ’s Exiles, see JJ to Pound, 5 June 1917, notes.

Pound wrote JJ on 17 July 1917: “I wish I believed more in ‘Exiles’, but damn it all, I dont think it up to the rest of your stuff.” He added that the play would not “build up your position, or help your next novel” (Pound/Joyce 122). With sensitive insight, Pound confided to John Quinn that “after [JJ’s] troubles with Dubliners and Portrait, I dont suppose anything will convince him that endless refusals of a mss. mean anything” (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1991], 124).
JJ wrote a limerick on Quinn’s “lavish largesse” but lack of appreciation for Exiles (Ellmann, JJ 413).

Grant Richards stated this in a letter to JJ dated 16 July 1917 (Robert Scholes, “Grant Richard to James Joyce,” Studies in Bibliography, vol. 16 [1963]: 159). In the end, Richards in London and B.W. Huebsch in New York published Exiles in May 1918.

Grant Richards wrote JJ on 16 July 1917 with regard to his planned publication of Exiles: “[G]etting proofs from printers is a difficult job in these days. They are all working with depleted staffs” (Scholes, “Grant Richard to James Joyce,” 159).

JJ had written his London literary agent J. B. Pinker on 8 July 1917 with instructions about getting Exiles prepared for publication by Grant Richards (LII 398). On 15 August 1917, Pinker wrote JJ that he had still not been able to settle the details of the contract with Richards, adding, “You know how difficult he is to pin down” (John Firth, “James Pinker to James Joyce, 1915–1920,” Studies in Bibliography 21 [1968]: 221).
Pound wrote JJ on 17 July 1917 that “it will ease your mind to have [Exiles] in print, and off your chest” (Pound/Joyce 122).

JJ wrote John Quinn a long letter on 10 July 1917 recounting his difficulties in getting Dubliners published and Exiles produced for the stage, adding, “All refused to aid me, except Mr Ezra Pound” (LI 104-05).

JJ reported to John Quinn on 10 July 1917 that A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man was “[f]inancially … like my other books, a fiasco – 450 copies sold to date in the United Kingdom, equivalent to a sale of about 28 copies in all Switzerland” (LI 105). Later the same month, JJ received a check for royalties, minus his agent’s commission, in the amount of £15.4.0 (LI 106).
For the early reviews of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, see JJ to Pound, 30 March 1917, notes.
On 5 June 1917, JJ reported to Pound that he had finished drafts of “Lotus-Eaters” and “Hades” and was assembling notes for “Aeolus” – respectively the fifth, sixth, and seventh episodes of Ulysses.

JJ enclosed four closely printed pages titled “Extract From Press Notices Of A Portrait Of The Artist As A Young Man By James Joyce (The Egoist, Ltd.: London: 1916).” Leading off with Pound, the extract included a total of thirty-one notices by H.G. Wells, Ernest Boyd, and others, with numerous uncredited notices from English, Irish, and Scottish newspapers. These anonymous newspaper notices varied wildly from the Glasgow Herald’s judgment that JJ was a “remarkable writer” to Everyman’s conclusion that A Portrait was a “study in garbage.” The Dublin Freeman’s Journal opined that “Mr. Joyce plunges and drags his readers after him into the slime of foul sewers …. His pen, instead of pointing to the stars overhead, is degraded into a muck-rake.”
For the notice of A Portrait in Esperia, see JJ to Pound, 9 July 1917, notes.

Pavlos (Paul) G. Phocas, a Greek friend who was a member of a convivial group in Zurich calling themselves the Club des Étrangers. Joyce learned some modern Greek from Phocas and another Étranger member, Paul Ruggiero. Phocas’s lessons were as quirky as JJ’s own language pedagogy. For example, he assigned JJ phrases like “Excuse me, I have to go to the toilet” and “Pigs eat shit,” and a quatrain on the penis (see Manto Aravantinou, Ta elliniká tou James Joyce [Athens: Ermís, 1977]). Phocas translated JJ’s poem “Sleep now, O sleep now,” from Chamber Music, into modern Greek (JJII 407-08 & n.). In the “Cyclops” episode of Ulysses, “S. Phocas of Sinope” features in a parodic list of “saints and martyrs, virgins and confessors” (U 12.1690). A notebook of exercises in modern Greek compiled by JJ in Zurich (ca. 1915-1919) contains two letters from Phocas (Peter Spielberg, James Joyce’s Manuscripts and Letters at the University of Buffalo: A Catalogue [Buffalo, NY: University of Buffalo, 1962], 161).

Santa Mavra or Santa Maura (known today as Lefkas or Lefkada) is one of the Ionian Islands that include Ithaca and Corfu, off the west coast of Greece. The German archaeologist Wilhelm Dörpfeld (1853-1940) concluded that Homer’s Ithaca was actually Santa Mavra; and Walter Leaf adopted this theory in Homer and History (London: Macmillan, 1915), 143-57, and other writings. Leaf, like Victor Bérard (1864-1931) whose theories JJ also encountered around this time, insisted that Homer based his epics “on actual geography, and did not invent” (157).
The office of the London weekly Hesperia was at 62 Oxford Street. JJ accidentally mailed his note of thanks to 62 Chancery Lane (LI 17).

Pound was acquainted with Henry D. Davray (1873-1944), a French critic who contributed regularly on English literature to the Mercure de France and had reviewed Pound’s book Spirit of Romance (1910) in its pages.

Pound wrote JJ on 17 July 1917 that Davray, with whom he had spoken, promised to review JJ’s work in the Mercure “when he gets leisure” (Pound/Joyce 122). JJ wrote Harriet Shaw Weaver on 1 December 1918 that no article by Davray had yet appeared, “but the century is still young” (LI 122). Davray’s article, “Lettres anglaises,” discussing JJ’s Exiles and other writings, was published in the Mercure, vol. 121, no. 495 (1 February 1919): 512-18. Davray wrote that in Exiles JJ had exposed the destructive influence of Tolstoy and other Russians on modern intellectuals “deprived of a sense of reality and of social conscience” and “liberated from the natural basis which furnishes them with the bonds of family, of nation, and of state” (Robert H. Deming, ed., James Joyce: The Critical Heritage, Volume 1, 1907-1927 [London: Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1970], 154-55). JJ wrote Davray on 17 June 1919 to thank him for “l’article très bienveillant et flatteur” (“the very benevolent and flattering article”) (LII 443).

William Archer (1856-1924), Scottish writer and critic, was an advocate of the drama of Henrik Ibsen and George Bernard Shaw. As a young man, JJ was overwhelmed to learn from Archer that Ibsen had appreciated the article on When We Dead Awaken that JJ had published in the Fortnightly Review in 1900. Ellmann states that despite JJ’s requests for help with Exiles, Archer “does not seem to have done anything,” and did not care much for JJ’s “form of realism” in A Portrait (Ellmann, JJ 415-16).

Arthur Symons (1865-1945), British poet and critic, met JJ through W.B. Yeats in 1902. He recommended JJ’s Chamber Music to the London publisher Elkin Mathews and praised the published volume in The Nation (London), vol. 1, no. 17 (22 June 1907): 639.

Probably Pieter or Piet Endt (1883-1936), a Dutch sociologist, translator, and novelist who earned his doctorate in political economy at the University of Zurich in 1918, and wrote on labor and the laboring classes in Indonesia. He was also a songwriter and chansonnier in the Netherlands and had toured the Dutch East Indies in 1916. Under the pseudonyms “Herman Fairfax” and “Eduard Coenraads,” he translated works by George Bernard Shaw, Friedrich Nietzsche, Gerhart Hauptmann, and W. Somerset Maugham. As “Eduard Coenraads,” he published two novels in Dutch, Island of Happiness (1920) and Torch Bearers (1923) (https://robscholtemuseum.nl/janet-wasserman-han-van-meegeren-and-his-portraits-of-theo-van-der-pas-and-jopie-breemer-3/).
Letters written by Endt to JJ from July and September 1917 indicate that he had composed what he called a “Dutch letter” which he intended to send directly to Amsterdam rather than through J.T. Grein in London (see note 34, below), as possibly quicker. This letter was probably related to Endt’s review of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, published under his pseudonym “Ed. Coenraads” in the Amsterdam literary paper, De Nieuwe Gids (The New Guide), vol. 33, no. 10 (1918): 516-19. The piece was titled “Een Ierse schrijver” (“An Irish Writer”) and carried the dateline “Zurich, January ’18.” In the review, Endt comments on the unwillingness of Irish and English (and Dutch) readers to accept frank, naturalistic treatments of art and life, except when forced to do so by foreign authors and critics such as the Irishman George Bernard Shaw and the Dutchman J.T. Grein, “who fought for revolutionary foreign art in their London newspaper reviews: for Wagner, for Ibsen” (516). Oscar Wilde, too, brought a Flaubertian directness to English readers. “And now it’s an Irishman again [JJ], bringing a novel written in English, but not an English novel. Not a book by Hardy, Kipling or Hall Caine” (“En nu is het weer een Ier, die een roman brengt in de Engelse taal geschreven, maar geen Engelse roman. Geen boek van Hardy, Kipling of Hall Caine”) (516-17). “‘When I’m about to read a book by an Englishman’ – Joyce once told me – ‘I feel as though I’ve been invited to a supper where I have to sit with all kinds of masked women and men’” (“‘Als ik een boek van een Engelsman ga lezen’ – zei Joyce mij eens – ‘dan heb ik het gevoel alsof ik uitgenoodigd ben aan een souper, waar ik aanzitten moet met allemaal gemaskerde vrouwen en mannen’”) (517).
Endt goes on to describe the refusal of English printers to set A Portrait and the necessity of importing sheets from America for the first Egoist Press edition in England. “Every page of Zola provides more sensational naturalistic details than this austere Irish word artist. And yet it seems to be too powerful for an Englishman. ‘Too many smells’” (“Iedere pagina van Zola geeft sensationeler naturalistiese details dan deze sobere Ierse woordkunstenaar. En toch schijnt het voor een Engelsman nog te machtig te zijn. ‘Too many smells’”) (517). Endt notes JJ’s “impressionistic” rendering of a Catholic boarding school, the terrible sermon on Hell to which Stephen is subjected, his religious exercises and self-mortifications, and his experience of watching the bird-girl at the seashore. Of this latter scene Endt remarks: “Joyce juxtaposes things as in a strange futuristic painting … but without any direct connection of the lovingly painted details; without accented development. The growth [of Stephen] is indicated, nowhere explained. Fragments from the life of Stephen Dedalus, the shy boy; nuggets under wonderful light” (“Joyce zet de dingen naast elkaar als een vreemd futuristies schilderij … maar zonder dadelik verband der in liefde gepenseelde details; zonder geakcentueerde ontwikkeling. De groei wordt aangeduid, nergens verklaard. Fragmenten uit het leven van Stephen Dedalus, de schuwe jongen; brokken onder wonderlik-vallend licht” (518).
J.T. (Jacob Thomas) Grein (1862-1935), an influential theatre producer and critic in London, of Dutch origin. See JJ to Pound, 30 March 1917, notes.

In these verses, JJ declares his indifference to the slights of journalists and publishers (“press and pressman”) as long as he can live creatively in the world of Ulysses, his modern Odyssey set in Dublin, with Leopold and Molly Bloom as his companions. These lines may have been offered in exchange for twelve lines “mistranslating Horace” that Pound included in his letter to JJ of 17 July 1917 (Pound/Joyce 122-23). There may also be a hint of resentment towards Pound, who had reiterated in the 17 July letter his lack of enthusiasm for Exiles. Some years later, JJ recorded a dream about Leopold and Molly Bloom in which there was a sudden “shout of laughter from some American journalists … led by Ezra Pound” (Ellmann, JJ 549). As in the dream, these verses may hint at JJ’s irritation with Pound the journalist, a role Pound actively played for much of his career, both as writer and editor.
